item.title: Training & Inference
item.description:
LLM training optimization spans distributed parallelization, memory management, kernel-level execution, numerical precision, and algorithmic architecture.

Medium

1. Distributed Parallelism Strategies

  • Tensor Parallelism (TP): Splits individual matrix multiplications across GPUs within a single node (e.g., Megatron-LM splitting MLP and Attention weight matrices column-wise and row-wise). Requires low-latency interconnects (NVLink).
  • Pipeline Parallelism (PP): Partitions layers sequentially across multiple nodes (e.g., GPipe, Megatron-LM 1F1B schedule). Uses micro-batching to reduce pipeline bubbles.
  • Context Parallelism (CP / RingAttention): Shards the sequence dimension across devices to process ultra-long contexts (64k+64\text{k}+64k+ to 1M+1\text{M}+1M+ tokens) without exhausting single-device memory.
  • Expert Parallelism (EP): For Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, routes token embeddings dynamically to specialized feed-forward experts partitioned across different ranks via All-to-All communication.
  • 3D/4D Parallelism: Combines DP, TP, PP, and CP to scale training across tens of thousands of GPUs.

2. Memory Reduction & Sharding

  • ZeRO (Zero Redundancy Optimizer) / FSDP:
    • Stage 1: Shards optimizer states across data-parallel ranks (saves ≈4×\approx 4\times≈4× memory).
    • Stage 2: Shards optimizer states and gradients (saves ≈8×\approx 8\times≈8× memory).
    • Stage 3 / Full FSDP: Shards optimizer states, gradients, and model parameters. Dynamically gathers parameters on-demand during forward/backward passes and discards them immediately.
  • Activation / Gradient Checkpointing: Discards intermediate forward-pass activations and recomputes them during the backward pass, trading ∼20–30%\sim 20\text{–}30\%∼20–30% compute overhead for drastic activation memory reduction.
  • Selective Activation Recomputation: Recomputes only memory-heavy, compute-cheap operations (such as attention score softmax/dropout) while caching compute-heavy GEMM activations.
  • CPU / NVMe Offloading (ZeRO-Offload): Offloads optimizer states and infrequently accessed weights from high-bandwidth HBM to host memory during step updates.

3. Kernel & Compute Acceleration

  • FlashAttention (v1, v2, v3): IO-aware tiling algorithms that compute exact scaled dot-product attention in fast on-chip SRAM. Avoids materializing the O(N2)O(N^2)O(N2) attention matrix in high-bandwidth memory (HBM), drastically cutting memory bandwidth bottlenecks.
  • Operator Fusion: Merges adjacent pointwise, normalization, and linear operations (e.g., RMSNorm + GEMM, SwiGLU, fused AdamW) to eliminate redundant kernel launches and intermediate global-memory round-trips.
  • Deep Learning Compilers: Frameworks like PyTorch Dynamo/torch.compile, Triton, and XLA generate optimized, hardware-specific C++/CUDA kernels with automatic layout transformations and graph fusions.
  • Communication Overlap: Hides collective communication overhead (AllReduce, ReduceScatter, AllGather) behind independent compute kernels using CUDA streams and double-buffering.

4. Precision & Numerical Formats

  • Mixed Precision (AMP with BF16 / FP16): Stores weights, activations, and gradients in 16-bit while tracking optimizer states and weight master copies in FP32. BF16 is preferred over FP16 due to its dynamic range matching FP32, eliminating manual loss scaling.
  • FP8 Training: Utilizes E4M3 (forward activations/weights) and E5M2 (backward gradients) formats supported on newer accelerator architectures (Hopper, Blackwell) to halve HBM footprints and double Tensor Core throughput.
  • Stochastic Rounding: Mitigates gradient underflow and quantization error when accumulating low-bit gradient updates into low-precision master weights.

5. Architectural & Algorithmic Optimizations

  • Attention Variants:
    • Multi-Query Attention (MQA) & Grouped-Query Attention (GQA): Shares key/value projections across heads, decreasing memory traffic and cache footprint during autoregressive rollout and training.
      • Sliding Window / Local Attention: Restricts attention computation to a localized context window.
  • Optimizers:
    • Memory-Efficient Optimizers: Adafactor, Lion, and 8-bit Adam (bitsandbytes) compress or factorize optimizer second-moment accumulators from 8 bytes/param down to 1–2 bytes/param.
      • Muon / Shampoo: Second-order or orthogonalized momentum optimizers that accelerate convergence per token compared to standard AdamW.
  • Data Packing: Concatenates multiple short token sequences into a single fixed-length window separated by attention masks to eliminate padding-token compute waste.
  • Curriculum & Variable-Length Batching: Schedules sequence lengths progressively (e.g., training on 2k2\text{k}2k tokens before expanding to 8k+8\text{k}\text{+}8k+) to minimize compute early in training.

6. Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT)

When adapting pre-trained models rather than pretraining from scratch:

Method Mechanism Parameter Footprint
LoRA / QLoRA Injects low-rank decomposition matrices (W0+BAW_0+BAW0​+BA) into attention/MLP layers; QLoRA quantizes the base model to 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4). ≪1%\ll 1\%≪1% trainable params
DoRA Decomposes weight matrices into magnitude and directional components, applying LoRA solely to the direction vector. ≪1%\ll 1\%≪1% trainable params
Prefix Tuning / Prompt Tuning Prepends trainable continuous virtual tokens to key/value or input embeddings. <0.1%<0.1\%<0.1% trainable params

item.title: Chinchilla derivation
item.description:
Here is a clean, rigorous step-by-step mathematical derivation of why scaling laws take the form of power laws, and why the 1:1 Chinchilla ratio emerges theoretically.

Part 1: Why Loss Follows a Power Law (L∝N−αL \propto N^{-\alpha}L∝N−α)

The power-law relationship between parameters NNN and loss LLL can be derived directly from manifold geometry and kernel spectral theory.

1. The Geometric Cover Argument

Assume human language exists on a ddd-dimensional manifold (surface) embedded within a higher-dimensional vector space.

  1. Space Partitioning: A neural network with NNN parameters can partition this ddd-dimensional manifold into NNN distinct region cells (or “boxes”) to approximate the true language distribution.
  2. Cell Radius: The volume of the entire manifold is constant. Dividing it into NNN equal cells means each cell has a volume Vcell∝1NV_{\text{cell}} \propto \frac{1}{N}Vcell​∝N1​.
  3. Linear Characteristic Length (ϵ\epsilonϵ): Since volume in ddd dimensions scales as length to the ddd-th power (V∝ϵdV \propto \epsilon^dV∝ϵd), the average linear diameter ϵ\epsilonϵ of each cell is: ϵ∝(1N)1d=N−1d \epsilon \propto \left(\frac{1}{N}\right)^{\frac{1}{d}} = N^{-\frac{1}{d}} ϵ∝(N1​)d1​=N−d1​
  4. Approximation Loss: For smooth functions, the local error (loss) inside a cell of size ϵ\epsilonϵ scales quadratically or linearly with the cell size ϵ\epsilonϵ (via Taylor expansion): L(N)−L∞∝ϵβ L(N) - L_{\infty} \propto \epsilon^\beta L(N)−L∞​∝ϵβ where L∞L_{\infty}L∞​ is the irreducible entropy of language, and β≥1\beta \ge 1β≥1 depends on the smoothness of the model.
  5. The Power-Law Exponent: Substituting ϵ∝N−1/d\epsilon \propto N^{-1/d}ϵ∝N−1/d into the error equation gives: L(N)−L∞∝(N−1d)β=N−βd L(N) - L_{\infty} \propto \left(N^{-\frac{1}{d}}\right)^\beta = N^{-\frac{\beta}{d}} L(N)−L∞​∝(N−d1​)β=N−dβ​

Setting αN=βd\alpha_N = \frac{\beta}{d}αN​=dβ​ yields the empirical parameter scaling law:

L(N)−L∞=A⋅N−αN L(N) - L_{\infty} = A \cdot N^{-\alpha_N} L(N)−L∞​=A⋅N−αN​

Key Takeaway: The scaling exponent αN\alpha_NαN​ reflects the ratio of network smoothness (β\betaβ) to the intrinsic dimensionality (ddd) of natural language. Because text has a high intrinsic dimension ddd, αN\alpha_NαN​ is a small fraction (typically 0.050.050.05 to 0.340.340.34).

Part 2: Formulating the Joint Loss Function L(N,D)L(N, D)L(N,D)

When training with both finite parameters (NNN) and finite tokens (DDD), the model faces two independent sources of error:

  1. Representation Error (A⋅N−αA \cdot N^{-\alpha}A⋅N−α): Bottleneck from having too few parameters to store patterns.
  2. Estimation Error (B⋅D−βB \cdot D^{-\beta}B⋅D−β): Bottleneck from seeing too few data samples to estimate parameters accurately (variance from Stochastic Gradient Descent).

Assuming these two errors are additive alongside the irreducible loss (EEE), the joint loss equation formulated in the Chinchilla paper is:

L(N,D)=E+ANα+BDβ L(N, D) = E + \frac{A}{N^\alpha} + \frac{B}{D^\beta} L(N,D)=E+NαA​+DβB​
  • EEE: Irreducible loss (entropy of true natural language).
  • A,BA, BA,B: Constants related to data distribution scale.
  • α,β\alpha, \betaα,β: Empirical exponents governing parameter and data efficiency (α≈0.34\alpha \approx 0.34α≈0.34, β≈0.28\beta \approx 0.28β≈0.28).

item.title: Scaling laws
item.description:
The two foundational papers that established and refined LLM scaling laws are:

  1. Kaplan et al. (OpenAI, 2020): “Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models” GitHub
  2. Hoffmann et al. (DeepMind, 2022): “Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models” (commonly known as the Chinchilla paper) Analytics Vidhya

Below is a detailed synthesis of all the major insights from both papers.

1. Kaplan et al. (OpenAI, 2020) Insights

Kaplan et al. provided the first empirical foundation showing that language model performance improves predictably according to strict power laws across many orders of magnitude.

Key Insights:

  • Performance is highly predictable: Test loss (LLL) scales smoothly as a power law with compute budget (CCC), model size (NNN), and dataset size (DDD): GitHub L(N)∝N−αN,L(D)∝D−αD,L(C)∝C−αC L(N) \propto N^{-\alpha_N}, \quad L(D) \propto D^{-\alpha_D}, \quad L(C) \propto C^{-\alpha_C} L(N)∝N−αN​,L(D)∝D−αD​,L(C)∝C−αC​
  • Architecture shape barely matters: Specific design details—such as depth vs. width, feed-forward dimensions, or number of attention heads—have minimal effect on final performance compared to overall parameter count. GitHub
  • Bigger models are more sample-efficient: Larger models learn faster and achieve a target loss using fewer total tokens than smaller models. GitHub
  • “Bigger is Better” allocation (The Flaw): Kaplan et al. concluded that when compute increases, most of the new budget should go toward increasing model size (NNN), while data size (DDD) needs to grow only slowly. arXiv
    • Their rule: Increase model size by ∼73%\sim 73\%∼73% and dataset size by only ∼27%\sim 27\%∼27% for each doubling of compute.
  • Early stopping & undertraining: They suggested it is optimal to train massive models for relatively few steps and stop training long before full convergence. GitHub
  • Downstream capability gap: Smooth, continuous scaling predicts cross-entropy loss improvement, but does not explicitly predict qualitative “emergent” capabilities (like few-shot reasoning).

2. Hoffmann et al. / Chinchilla (DeepMind, 2022) Insights

DeepMind re-examined Kaplan et al.’s findings by training over 400 models (ranging from 70M to 16B parameters on up to 500B tokens). They discovered that OpenAI’s original learning rate schedules and hyperparameter setups artificially penalized smaller models trained on large token counts, leading to flawed conclusions.

GitHub

Key Insights:

  • The 1:1 Equal Scaling Law: For optimal training compute efficiency, model size (NNN) and training data (DDD) must scale at equal rates (1:1).
    • If you double the compute budget, you should double both the parameter count and the number of tokens. Analytics Vidhya
  • The ~20:1 Golden Ratio: A model trained to compute-optimal efficiency requires roughly 20 tokens per parameter (D≈20ND \approx 20ND≈20N). Analytics Vidhya
  • Massive LLMs were severely undertrained: Most high-profile LLMs built between 2020 and 2022 (e.g., GPT-3, Gopher, Megatron-Turing NLG) were far too large relative to the amount of data they were trained on. Michael Brenndoerfer
  • Proof with Chinchilla (70B): DeepMind built Chinchilla, a 70B parameter model trained on 1.4 trillion tokens. Despite having 2.5×2.5\times2.5× fewer parameters than GPT-3 (175B) and Gopher (280B), Chinchilla outperformed both models across virtually every benchmark while using substantially less training compute. Analytics Vidhya
  • Mathematical Loss Equation: They formalized the loss function incorporating an irreducible loss (EEE): L(N,D)=E+ANα+BDβ L(N, D) = E + \frac{A}{N^\alpha} + \frac{B}{D^\beta} L(N,D)=E+NαA​+DβB​ where optimal parameters scale as Nopt∝CaN_{opt} \propto C^aNopt​∝Ca and Dopt∝CbD_{opt} \propto C^bDopt​∝Cb, finding a≈0.5a \approx 0.5a≈0.5 and b≈0.5b \approx 0.5b≈0.5.

Direct Comparison & Modern Impact

Metric / Dimension Kaplan et al. (OpenAI 2020) Hoffmann et al. / Chinchilla (DeepMind 2022)
Compute Scaling Strategy Favor Model Size (N∝C0.73N\propto C^{0.73}N∝C0.73) over Data (D∝C0.27D\propto C^{0.27}D∝C0.27) Equal Proportional Scaling (N∝C0.5N\propto C^{0.5}N∝C0.5, D∝C0.5D\propto C^{0.5}D∝C0.5)
Token-to-Parameter Ratio ~1.7 to 5 tokens per parameter ~20 tokens per parameter
Model Paradigm Example GPT-3 (175B params, 300B tokens) Chinchilla (70B params, 1.4T tokens)
Primary Takeaway Train larger models and stop early. Train smaller models on much more data.

Legacy & Post-Chinchilla Era:

  • Inference-Optimal Over-training: While Chinchilla defined compute-optimal training, modern open-weights models (like Llama 3 8B trained on 15T+ tokens—a 1,800:1 ratio) intentionally break Chinchilla laws. They pay a higher training cost upfront to get a smaller model that is substantially cheaper and faster to run at inference across millions of user

item.title: Llm training variants
item.description:
These pre-training objectives teach language models syntax, semantics, and context by predicting corrupted, omitted, or shifted parts of text.

Autoregressive & Prefix Models

  • Causal LM (Causal Language Modeling): Predicts the next token strictly from left to right using directional masking (standard GPT architecture). Each token only attends to preceding tokens.
  • Prefix LM: Allows full bidirectional attention over an initial prompt (“prefix”), then switches to standard autoregressive causal generation to predict the continuation (e.g., T5 decoder/prefix mode).

Masking & Denoising Objectives

  • Masked LM (MLM): Masks random tokens with a special tag (e.g., [MASK]) and trains the model to predict the original hidden words using bidirectional context (BERT-style).
  • BERT-style MLM: An implementation detail of MLM where masked positions are replaced 80% of the time with [MASK], 10% with a random token, and 10% kept unchanged, forcing the model to evaluate all token representations.
  • MASS-style (Masked Sequence to Sequence): Masks a contiguous span of tokens in the encoder, and uses the decoder to autoregressively reconstruct only the masked segment.
  • Span Masking: Instead of masking individual words at random, masks contiguous sequences of tokens (spans) to make recovery harder and force deeper context comprehension (e.g., SpanBERT).
  • Sentinel Masking (Span Corruption): Replaces entire masked spans with unique sentinel tokens (e.g., <extra_id_0>, <extra_id_1>), training the decoder to output only the sentinels followed by their missing spans (used by T5).

Sequence & Permutation Objectives

  • Permuted LM (PLM): Samples random factorization orders for predicting tokens while keeping standard positional embeddings, capturing bidirectional context without introducing artificial [MASK] tokens (used by XLNet).
  • Token Classification: Predicts a label (such as Part-of-Speech or Named Entity) for every single token representation simultaneously.
  • Token Deletion: Deletes random tokens entirely without leaving mask tokens; the model must reconstruct the full missing sequence (BART denoising).
  • Token Reordering: Randomly shuffles tokens in the input and trains the model to generate them in the correct original order.

Sentence & Document-Level Objectives

  • Next Sentence Prediction (NSP): Feeds two sentences and predicts whether the second sentence logically follows the first in the original text (BERT pre-training).
  • Sentence Comparison: Computes sentence embeddings to output a similarity score determining semantic equivalence or entailment (used in bi-encoders like SBERT).
  • Sentence Reordering: Shuffles the order of full sentences in a paragraph; the model must reconstruct the correct logical paragraph flow.
  • Document Rotation: Selects a random token as a rotation point and wraps the beginning of the text to the end; the model must locate the true start and restore the document.

item.description:
Attention mechanisms can be organized into six structural paradigms: classical scoring alignments, routing configurations, KV-cache parameter sharing, sparse & linear asymptotic reductions, hardware-aware tiling engines, and hierarchical multi-scale compressed attentions (including DeepSeek’s recent architectures).

1. Mathematical Scoring Functions (Compatibility Metrics)

Given query q∈Rdkq \in \mathbb{R}^{d_k}q∈Rdk​ and key k∈Rdkk \in \mathbb{R}^{d_k}k∈Rdk​:

  • Additive / Concat Attention (Bahdanau et al.): eij=vaTtanh⁡(Wqqi+Wkkj) e_{ij} = v_a^T \tanh(W_q q_i + W_k k_j) eij​=vaT​tanh(Wq​qi​+Wk​kj​) Maps queries and keys into a shared latent space before projecting down to a scalar via vav_ava​. High expressivity, but non-vectorized addition makes it memory-bound on tensor cores.
  • General / Bilinear Attention (Luong et al.): eij=qiTWakj e_{ij} = q_i^T W_a k_j eij​=qiT​Wa​kj​ Uses a learnable matrix Wa∈Rdq×dkW_a \in \mathbb{R}^{d_q \times d_k}Wa​∈Rdq​×dk​ to model asymmetric cross-correlation between different latent dimensions.
  • Scaled Dot-Product Attention (Vaswani et al.): Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax(QKTdk+M)V \text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}} + M\right)V Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax(dk​​QKT​+M)V The dk\sqrt{d_k}dk​​ divisor stabilizes variance at ≈1\approx 1≈1, preventing the softmax distribution from saturating with near-zero gradients at large dimensions.
  • Cosine / Scaled-Cosine Attention: eij=qi⋅kj∥qi∥2∥kj∥2⋅τ e_{ij} = \frac{q_i \cdot k_j}{\Vert{}q_i\Vert{}_2 \Vert{}k_j\Vert{}_2 \cdot \tau} eij​=∥qi​∥2​∥kj​∥2​⋅τqi​⋅kj​​ Normalizes vector norms and scales by learnable temperature τ\tauτ. Used in Swin Transformer v2 and vision transformers to prevent extreme logit drift.

2. Contextual Routing & Information Flow

  • Self-Attention: Q,K,VQ, K, VQ,K,V are projected from the same hidden sequence H∈RN×dH \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d}H∈RN×d. Computes intra-sequence token interaction.
  • Cross-Attention: QQQ originates from target sequence HdecH_{\text{dec}}Hdec​, while K,VK, VK,V originate from source sequence HencH_{\text{enc}}Henc​: Q=HdecWQ,K=HencWK,V=HencWV Q = H_{\text{dec}} W_Q, \quad K = H_{\text{enc}} W_K, \quad V = H_{\text{enc}} W_V Q=Hdec​WQ​,K=Henc​WK​,V=Henc​WV​
  • Causal Masking: Imposes Mij=−∞M_{ij} = -\inftyMij​=−∞ for j>ij > ij>i. Enforces autoregressive token dependency (p(xt∣x<t)p(x_t \mid x_{\lt t})p(xt​∣x<t​)).

item.title: CSA and HCA
item.description:
Compressed Sparse Attention (CSA) is an attention architecture introduced in DeepSeek-V4 designed to scale sequence context to massive lengths (1M+ tokens) while addressing both the compute bottleneck and the KV-cache memory capacity bottleneck.

While standard DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) solves compute complexity by selecting a top-kkk subset of past tokens, the KV cache still scales linearly with the sequence length (O(L)O(L)O(L) cache capacity). CSA combines sequence compression with dynamic sparse routing to slash both memory footprint and FLOPs.

Core Idea: Dual-Stage Efficiency

CSA operates through a two-step reduction:

  1. Token Pooling / KV Compression (m:1m:1m:1): Adjacent tokens along the sequence dimension are compressed into compact, pooled KV blocks using learned weights. Outcome School
  2. Dynamic Sparse Selection (Top-k\text{Top-}kTop-k): Instead of evaluating full attention over all compressed blocks, a lightweight Lightning Indexer scores the compressed entries and routes attention only to the top-kkk most relevant blocks. Outcome School
Raw Tokens (L)
│
▼ [Learned Overlapping Pooling (m:1)]
Compressed KV Blocks (L / m)
│
▼ [Lightning Indexer Scoring + Top-k Selection]
Sparse High-Precision Attention (k blocks)

Mathematical Mechanism

1. Overlapping KV Compression

Rather than doing naive downsampling or non-overlapping striding (which causes sharp information loss at boundaries), CSA performs overlapping sequence pooling.

Hugging Face

  • The compressed KV state CbComp∈RcC_b^{\text{Comp}} \in \mathbb{R}^{c}CbComp​∈Rc for block bbb is computed as: CbComp=∑i=02m−1πb,i⋅(Hb⋅m+iWcomp) C_b^{\text{Comp}} = \sum_{i=0}^{2m-1} \pi_{b, i} \cdot \left( H_{b \cdot m + i} W^{\text{comp}} \right) CbComp​=i=0∑2m−1​πb,i​⋅(Hb⋅m+i​Wcomp)

This compresses the stored KV cache along the sequence length by a factor of mmm.

Outcome School

2. The Lightning Indexer on Compressed Blocks

To decide which compressed blocks query ttt should attend to, a lightweight indexer projects query HtH_tHt​ and the compressed cache CbCompC_b^{\text{Comp}}CbComp​ into low-dimensional index spaces (didx≪dd_{\text{idx}} \ll ddidx​≪d):

  • Query index projection: qt,hI=HtWq,hI∈Rdidx q_{t, h}^I = H_t W_{q, h}^I \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{idx}}} qt,hI​=Ht​Wq,hI​∈Rdidx​
  • Compressed key index projection: KbI=CbCompWkI∈Rdidx K_b^I = C_b^{\text{Comp}} W_{k}^I \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{idx}}} KbI​=CbComp​WkI​∈Rdidx​

The relevance score It,bI_{t, b}It,b​ between query ttt and compressed block bbb is computed across nhIn_h^InhI​ index heads with a gated activation (e.g., ReLU) and learnable head weights wt,hIw_{t, h}^Iwt,hI​:

It,b=∑h=1nhIwt,hI⋅ReLU⁡(qt,hI⋅KbI) I_{t, b} = \sum_{h=1}^{n_h^I} w_{t, h}^I \cdot \operatorname{ReLU}\left( q_{t, h}^I \cdot K_b^I \right) It,b​=h=1∑nhI​​wt,hI​⋅ReLU(qt,hI​⋅KbI​)

Because scoring operates over Lm\frac{L}{m}mL​ entries in reduced precision (such as FP8/FP4) and low rank, index evaluation requires negligible compute compared to standard attention.

3. Top-kkk Sparse Attention

High-precision multi-head attention is then computed only against the retrieved kkk compressed entries:

Architectural Context: CSA vs. HCA

Outcome School

In architectures like DeepSeek-V4, CSA is typically interleaved with Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA):

Outcome School

Attention Type Compression Ratio (mmm) Selection Strategy Attention Density Purpose
CSA Mild (m=4m=4m=4) Dynamic Top-kkk via Indexer Sparse High-detail retrieval over relevant history.
HCA Aggressive (m′=128m'=128m′=128) None (No indexer) Dense Global background context with near-zero cache footprint.

Summary of Benefits

  • Reduced KV Footprint: Compressing mmm tokens into 1 entry shrinks the physical memory consumption of the KV cache by m×m\timesm×. Outcome School
  • Sub-linear Scaling: With kkk fixed (e.g., k≪L/mk \ll L/mk≪L/m), the computational cost of the main attention core scales with O(k⋅d)O(k \cdot d)O(k⋅d) instead of O(L⋅d)O(L \cdot d)O(L⋅d).
  • No Boundary Artifacts: The 2m2m2m overlapping softmax pooling prevents rigid chunking boundaries from destroying local syntactic and semantic cohesion.

DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) is a dynamic, content-dependent sparse attention mechanism designed to bypass the standard quadratic attention cost O(L2)O(L^2)O(L2) for long sequences without relying on rigid, pre-defined static patterns (such as fixed sliding windows or static strided blocks).

Medium

Instead of attending to all LLL tokens, DSA uses a two-stage pipeline:

  1. A Lightning Indexer cheaply scans all past tokens to score their relevance for each query token. Emergent Mind
  2. A Top-kkk Selector gathers the highest-scoring kkk key-value entries (k≪Lk \ll Lk≪L, typically k≈2048k \approx 2048k≈2048 out of 128K+128\text{K}+128K+ context) to run the full-fidelity Multi-Head / Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA).

The Lightning Indexer: Mathematical Formulation

In standard full attention, computing attention weights requires projecting hidden states into dimension dkd_kdk​, performing an inner product QK⊤/dkQ K^\top / \sqrt{d_k}QK⊤/dk​​, and materializing an L×LL \times LL×L attention matrix.

The Lightning Indexer avoids this bottleneck by performing scoring in a low-dimensional space using lightweight numerical formats (FP8).

item.title: MLA
item.description:
Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA), introduced by DeepSeek, solves a core bottleneck in Transformer inference: the massive size and memory bandwidth cost of the KV Cache.

Chris McCormick

While Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) reduces KV heads at the cost of model expressiveness, MLA achieves extreme compression without losing representational capacity by using low-rank latent projections and algebraic weight absorption.

Chris McCormick

1. Why Standard Multi-Head Attention (MHA) Is Costly

For an input token vector xt∈Rd\mathbf{x}_t \in \mathbb{R}^dxt​∈Rd across nhn_hnh​ heads, each head generates query, key, and value vectors of dimension dhd_hdh​:

qt,i=xtWiQ,kt,i=xtWiK,vt,i=xtWiV(i=1,…,nh) \mathbf{q}_{t,i} = \mathbf{x}_t \mathbf{W}_i^Q, \quad \mathbf{k}_{t,i} = \mathbf{x}_t \mathbf{W}_i^K, \quad \mathbf{v}_{t,i} = \mathbf{x}_t \mathbf{W}_i^V \quad (i = 1, \dots, n_h) qt,i​=xt​WiQ​,kt,i​=xt​WiK​,vt,i​=xt​WiV​(i=1,…,nh​)

During autoregressive generation, we must store all past keys and values in memory:

KV Cache per token=2×nh×dh numbers \text{KV Cache per token} = 2 \times n_h \times d_h \text{ numbers} KV Cache per token=2×nh​×dh​ numbers

For large models (e.g., 128 heads, head dimension 128), that is over 32,000 floats per token, dominating memory footprint and memory-bus bandwidth.

Chris McCormick

2. Multi-Head Latent Attention: Without RoPE

The central intuition of MLA is simple: instead of storing full multi-head keys and values, compress each token’s key and value representations into a single low-dimensional latent vector.

The Compression (Down-Projection)

Instead of projecting xt\mathbf{x}_txt​ directly to nhn_hnh​ heads, we down-project it into a compact latent vector ctKV∈Rdc\mathbf{c}_t^{KV} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_c}ctKV​∈Rdc​ where dc≪nh×dhd_c \ll n_h \times d_hdc​≪nh​×dh​:

ctKV=xtWDKV \mathbf{c}_t^{KV} = \mathbf{x}_t \mathbf{W}^{DKV} ctKV​=xt​WDKV
  • WDKV∈Rd×dc\mathbf{W}^{DKV} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d_c}WDKV∈Rd×dc​ is the down-projection matrix.
  • In the KV cache, we only store ctKV\mathbf{c}_t^{KV}ctKV​ (a single vector of size dcd_cdc​ per token, rather than 2⋅nh⋅dh2 \cdot n_h \cdot d_h2⋅nh​⋅dh​). Chris McCormick

(Queries are also compressed during training to save activation memory via ctQ=xtWDQ\mathbf{c}_t^Q = \mathbf{x}_t \mathbf{W}^{DQ}ctQ​=xt​WDQ, then up-projected to qt,i=ctQWiUQ\mathbf{q}_{t,i} = \mathbf{c}_t^Q \mathbf{W}_i^{UQ}qt,i​=ctQ​WiUQ​, though query compression does not affect KV cache sizing.)

Generation & The “Weight Absorption” Trick

To compute attention, keys and values for head iii are theoretically uncompressed using up-projection matrices:

kj,i=cjKVWiUK,vj,i=cjKVWiUV \mathbf{k}_{j,i} = \mathbf{c}_j^{KV} \mathbf{W}_i^{UK}, \quad \mathbf{v}_{j,i} = \mathbf{c}_j^{KV} \mathbf{W}_i^{UV} kj,i​=cjKV​WiUK​,vj,i​=cjKV​WiUV​

where WiUK∈Rdc×dh\mathbf{W}_i^{UK} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_c \times d_h}WiUK​∈Rdc​×dh​ and WiUV∈Rdc×dh\mathbf{W}_i^{UV} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_c \times d_h}WiUV​∈Rdc​×dh​.

The attention score between query token ttt and key token jjj for head iii is:

Scorei(t,j)=qt,ikj,iT=qt,i(cjKVWiUK)T=qt,i(WiUK)T(cjKV)T \text{Score}_{i}(t, j) = \mathbf{q}_{t,i} \mathbf{k}_{j,i}^T = \mathbf{q}_{t,i} \left( \mathbf{c}_j^{KV} \mathbf{W}_i^{UK} \right)^T = \mathbf{q}_{t,i} (\mathbf{W}_i^{UK})^T (\mathbf{c}_j^{KV})^T Scorei​(t,j)=qt,i​kj,iT​=qt,i​(cjKV​WiUK​)T=qt,i​(WiUK​)T(cjKV​)T

Because matrix multiplication is associative, we can group the terms differently:

Scorei(t,j)=(qt,i(WiUK)T)⏟qt,i′∈Rdc(cjKV)T \text{Score}_{i}(t, j) = \underbrace{\left(\mathbf{q}_{t,i} (\mathbf{W}_i^{UK})^T\right)}_{\mathbf{q}'_{t,i} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_c}} (\mathbf{c}_j^{KV})^T Scorei​(t,j)=qt,i′​∈Rdc​(qt,i​(WiUK​)T)​​(cjKV​)T

This provides a major performance optimization:

  1. Never decompress keys in memory: We project the single active query vector down into the latent space: qt,i′=qt,i(WiUK)T∈Rdc\mathbf{q}'_{t,i} = \mathbf{q}_{t,i} (\mathbf{W}_i^{UK})^T \in \mathbb{R}^{d_c}qt,i′​=qt,i​(WiUK​)T∈Rdc​.
  2. Compute the dot-product directly against the cached latent cjKV\mathbf{c}_j^{KV}cjKV​.
  3. For values, WiUV\mathbf{W}_i^{UV}WiUV​ can similarly be absorbed directly into the output projection WO\mathbf{W}^OWO.

3. The RoPE Problem

Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) injects relative token distance by rotating vectors with a position-dependent orthogonal matrix Rt\mathbf{R}_tRt​:

Outcome School

qt→qtRt,kj→kjRj \mathbf{q}_{t} \to \mathbf{q}_t \mathbf{R}_t, \quad \mathbf{k}_{j} \to \mathbf{k}_j \mathbf{R}_j qt​→qt​Rt​,kj​→kj​Rj​

If we apply standard RoPE to the decompressed key kj,i=cjKVWiUK\mathbf{k}_{j,i} = \mathbf{c}_j^{KV} \mathbf{W}_i^{UK}kj,i​=cjKV​WiUK​:

kj,iRoPE=cjKVWiUKRj \mathbf{k}_{j,i}^{\text{RoPE}} = \mathbf{c}_j^{KV} \mathbf{W}_i^{UK} \mathbf{R}_j kj,iRoPE​=cjKV​WiUK​Rj​

The attention dot-product becomes:

Scorei(t,j)=(qt,iRt)(kj,iRoPE)T=qt,iRtRjT(WiUK)T(cjKV)T \text{Score}_{i}(t, j) = (\mathbf{q}_{t,i} \mathbf{R}_t) (\mathbf{k}_{j,i}^{\text{RoPE}})^T = \mathbf{q}_{t,i} \mathbf{R}_t \mathbf{R}_j^T (\mathbf{W}_i^{UK})^T (\mathbf{c}_j^{KV})^T Scorei​(t,j)=(qt,i​Rt​)(kj,iRoPE​)T=qt,i​Rt​RjT​(WiUK​)T(cjKV​)T

Because RjT\mathbf{R}_j^TRjT​ sits squarely between WiUK\mathbf{W}_i^{UK}WiUK​ and cjKV\mathbf{c}_j^{KV}cjKV​, weight absorption breaks. You would either have to:

  • Decompress and rotate keys for every token in history at runtime (compute-prohibitive), or varmology
  • Cache the uncompressed, rotated keys across all heads (defeating the purpose of compressing the KV cache). varmology

4. Multi-Head Latent Attention: With Decoupled RoPE

MLA resolves this conflict by separating attention into two distinct parallel streams: a content stream and a position stream.

The Positional Pathway

  1. Decoupled Key: We project token xt\mathbf{x}_txt​ directly to a shared, low-dimensional position vector ktR∈RdR\mathbf{k}_t^R \in \mathbb{R}^{d_R}ktR​∈RdR​ (typically dR=64d_R = 64dR​=64), and apply rotation Rt\mathbf{R}_tRt​ to it: ktR=RoPE(xtWKR) \mathbf{k}_{t}^R = \text{RoPE}\left(\mathbf{x}_t \mathbf{W}^{KR}\right) ktR​=RoPE(xt​WKR) (Notice that all heads share this positional key or use a unified projection.) arXiv
  2. Decoupled Query: We project queries into both a content query qt,iC∈Rdh\mathbf{q}_{t,i}^C \in \mathbb{R}^{d_h}qt,iC​∈Rdh​ and a positional query qt,iR∈RdR\mathbf{q}_{t,i}^R \in \mathbb{R}^{d_R}qt,iR​∈RdR​: qt,iR=RoPE(ctQWiQR) \mathbf{q}_{t,i}^R = \text{RoPE}\left(\mathbf{c}_t^Q \mathbf{W}_i^{QR}\right) qt,iR​=RoPE(ctQ​WiQR​)

The Attention Score Calculation

The final query and key vectors are formed by concatenating their content and positional components:

qt,i=[qt,iC  ;  qt,iR],kj,i=[kj,iC  ;  kjR] \mathbf{q}_{t,i} = \left[ \mathbf{q}_{t,i}^C \;;\; \mathbf{q}_{t,i}^R \right], \quad \mathbf{k}_{j,i} = \left[ \mathbf{k}_{j,i}^C \;;\; \mathbf{k}_j^R \right] qt,i​=[qt,iC​;qt,iR​],kj,i​=[kj,iC​;kjR​]

The dot-product naturally splits into two additive terms:

Scorei(t,j)=qt,iC(kj,iC)T+qt,iR(kjR)T \text{Score}_{i}(t, j) = \mathbf{q}_{t,i}^C (\mathbf{k}_{j,i}^C)^T + \mathbf{q}_{t,i}^R (\mathbf{k}_j^R)^T Scorei​(t,j)=qt,iC​(kj,iC​)T+qt,iR​(kjR​)T

Substitute the content and RoPE representations:

Scorei(t,j)=(qt,iC(WiUK)T)⏟Absorbed: Rdc(cjKV)T+qt,iR(kjR)T⏟RoPE dot-product: RdR \text{Score}_{i}(t, j) = \underbrace{\left(\mathbf{q}_{t,i}^C (\mathbf{W}_i^{UK})^T\right)}_{\text{Absorbed: } \mathbb{R}^{d_c}} (\mathbf{c}_j^{KV})^T + \underbrace{\mathbf{q}_{t,i}^R (\mathbf{k}_j^R)^T}_{\text{RoPE dot-product: } \mathbb{R}^{d_R}} Scorei​(t,j)=Absorbed: Rdc​(qt,iC​(WiUK​)T)​​(cjKV​)T+RoPE dot-product: RdR​qt,iR​(kjR​)T​​
  • The content component retains full weight absorption—keys do not need to be uncompressed.
  • The position component is small (dR≈64d_R \approx 64dR​≈64) and decoupled from head-expansion. Chris McCormick

item.title: Pos Embeddings
item.description:
Self-attention in Transformers is permutation-equivariant: without position information, the model treats a sequence as an unordered bag of tokens. Positional encodings break this symmetry, giving tokens an address or a distance metric.

Abhik Sarkar

Positional embeddings in LLMs fall into three broad architectural families: Absolute, Relative, and Rotary / Bias-based hybrids.

1. Absolute Positional Embeddings (APE)

These assign a fixed or learned coordinate vector to each exact index (0,1,2,…,N0, 1, 2, \dots, N0,1,2,…,N) and add it directly to the token embedding before feeding it into the first transformer layer: xi=ei+pix_i = e_i + p_ixi​=ei​+pi​.

  • Sinusoidal Positional Encoding (Fixed APE):
    • Mechanism: Introduced in the original Transformer (Attention Is All You Need). Uses interleaved geometric sine and cosine waves across embedding dimensions: PE(pos,2i)=sin⁡(pos100002i/d),PE(pos,2i+1)=cos⁡(pos100002i/d) PE_{(pos, 2i)} = \sin\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d}}\right), \quad PE_{(pos, 2i+1)} = \cos\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d}}\right) PE(pos,2i)​=sin(100002i/dpos​),PE(pos,2i+1)​=cos(100002i/dpos​)
      • Strengths: Zero learned parameters; theoretically represents relative shifts via trigonometric identities.
      • Limitations: Added directly at the input, tangling positional information with semantic embeddings. Does not extrapolate reliably beyond the training sequence length. Wayland Zhang+ 1
  • Learned Absolute Embeddings:
    • Mechanism: Used in models like BERT, GPT-2, and OPT. Treats positions as a lookup table of trainable parameters matrix Wpos∈RLmax⁡×dW_{pos} \in \mathbb{R}^{L_{\max} \times d}Wpos​∈RLmax​×d.
      • Strengths: Adapts directly to the pretraining corpus data distribution.
      • Limitations: Hard ceiling on sequence length (Lmax⁡L_{\max}Lmax​). It cannot process token Lmax⁡+1L_{\max} + 1Lmax​+1 without structural alterations or interpolation.

2. Relative Positional Encodings (RPE)

Rather than caring where a token sits in the whole document, RPE cares about pairwise distance (i−j)(i - j)(i−j) between the query token iii and key token jjj.

liveBook · Manning - Manning Publications

  • Shaw’s Relative Positional Encoding:
    • Mechanism: Modifies the attention score and value aggregation by adding learned bias vectors corresponding to the clipped relative distance clip(i−j,−k,k)\text{clip}(i - j, -k, k)clip(i−j,−k,k).
      • Strengths: Translates easily across sequence lengths; reflects the intuition that local syntactic context matters more than global indices.
      • Limitations: Adds memory and compute overhead when forming per-head attention matrices; tricky to cache efficiently for fast autoregressive generation.
  • T5 Relative Bias:
    • Mechanism: Simplifies Shaw’s approach by directly adding a scalar bias bi−jb_{i-j}bi−j​ to the attention logit: Attentionij=qikj⊤d+bi−j \text{Attention}_{ij} = \frac{q_i k_j^\top}{\sqrt{d}} + b_{i-j} Attentionij​=d​qi​kj⊤​​+bi−j​ Positions are bucketed logarithmically so that nearby tokens have fine-grained distance bins, while far tokens share coarse bins.
      • Strengths: Extremely lightweight scalar addition; scales to long contexts with few parameters.
  • Transformer-XL / DeBERTa Relative Disentangled Encoding:
    • Mechanism: Decomposes attention into four disentangled terms: content-to-content, content-to-position, position-to-content, and position-to-position.
      • Strengths: Stronger representations for masked language modeling and natural language understanding.

3. Modern Multiplicative & Attention-Bias Methods

Modern autoregressive LLMs avoid adding vectors at the bottom layer, injecting position information directly into attention heads.

  • RoPE (Rotary Position Embedding):
    • Mechanism: Used by LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma, and DeepSeek. Instead of adding vectors, it rotates 2D slices of query and key vectors by an angle proportional to the position index mmm: qm=RΘ,mWqxm,kn=RΘ,nWkxn \mathbf{q}_m = \mathbf{R}_{\Theta, m} \mathbf{W}_q \mathbf{x}_m, \quad \mathbf{k}_n = \mathbf{R}_{\Theta, n} \mathbf{W}_k \mathbf{x}_n qm​=RΘ,m​Wq​xm​,kn​=RΘ,n​Wk​xn​ When computing qm⊤kn\mathbf{q}_m^\top \mathbf{k}_nqm⊤​kn​, the inner product naturally simplifies to an expression that depends purely on (m−n)(m - n)(m−n).
      • Strengths: Preserves vector norms, integrates with KV-caching with zero overhead, and allows context expansion via frequency scaling (e.g., RoPE-NTK, YaRN).
  • ALiBi (Attention with Linear Biases):
    • Mechanism: Used in BLOOM and MPT. Completely removes position embeddings. Instead, it adds a static, non-learned penalty proportional to distance directly to the attention logits: Attentioni,j=qikj⊤d−m⋅∣i−j∣ \text{Attention}_{i, j} = \frac{q_i k_j^\top}{\sqrt{d}} - m \cdot \vert{}i - j\vert{} Attentioni,j​=d​qi​kj⊤​​−m⋅∣i−j∣ where m=2−8h/Hm = 2^{-8h/H}m=2−8h/H is a fixed geometric slope unique to each attention head hhh.
      • Strengths: Zero learned position weights; achieves smooth zero-shot length extrapolation out of the box.
      • Limitations: Imposes a strict monotonic decay (local attention bias), which can hinder tasks needing long-range global reasoning. MetricGate
  • NoPE (No Positional Encoding):
    • Mechanism: Eliminates positional encodings entirely.
      • How it works: In causal decoder-only models, the autoregressive lower-triangular causal mask and causal scratchpad provide an implicit directional order.
      • Usage: Primarily used in research settings; performs surprisingly well on specific algorithmic and recurrent tasks, though it generally lags behind RoPE on standard natural language benchmarks.

Comparison Overview

Sinusoidal APE Input layer (Additive) Absolute Poor without scaling Original Transformer

ALiBi Attention logits (Linear penalty) Relative Very high (Zero-shot) BLOOM, MPT

item.title: RoPE
item.description:
Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) is a positional encoding mechanism for Transformer attention layers that represents position by rotating query and key vectors in high-dimensional space.

Outcome School

Introduced by Jianlin Su et al. (RoFormer), RoPE encodes absolute position via a rotation operation, while ensuring the inner product between query and key vectors naturally measures relative positional distance.

Michael Brenndoerfer

The Intuition

In standard attention, positional information is either:

  1. Added to inputs (x+pmx + p_mx+pm​), which entangles semantics with coordinates and dilutes deeper in the network.
  2. Injected as relative distance biases into attention logits, which can add computational overhead and break clean KV-cache management.

RoPE takes a geometric approach:

  • Imagine a 2D plane. If you have two vectors q\mathbf{q}q and k\mathbf{k}k, rotating q\mathbf{q}q by an angle α\alphaα and k\mathbf{k}k by β\betaβ changes their dot product based strictly on the difference β−α\beta - \alphaβ−α.
  • The length (norm) of the vectors is preserved because rotations are orthogonal transformations. TensorTonic
  • By scaling the rotation angle proportionally to a token’s index, token interactions depend directly on how far apart they are in the sequence. Medium

Mathematical Formulation

1. The 2D Case

For a 2D vector x=[x1,x2]T\mathbf{x} = [x_1, x_2]^Tx=[x1​,x2​]T at token index mmm, RoPE applies a 2D orthogonal rotation matrix RΘ,m\mathbf{R}_{\Theta, m}RΘ,m​:

RΘ,m=(cos⁡(mθ)−sin⁡(mθ)sin⁡(mθ)cos⁡(mθ)) \mathbf{R}_{\Theta, m} = \begin{pmatrix} \cos(m\theta) & -\sin(m\theta) \\ \sin(m\theta) & \cos(m\theta) \end{pmatrix} RΘ,m​=(cos(mθ)sin(mθ)​−sin(mθ)cos(mθ)​)

Equivalently, treating (x1,x2)(x_1, x_2)(x1​,x2​) as a complex number z=x1+ix2z = x_1 + i x_2z=x1​+ix2​:

xm′=z⋅eimθ \mathbf{x}'_m = z \cdot e^{i m \theta} xm′​=z⋅eimθ

When computing the dot product between query q\mathbf{q}q at position mmm and key k\mathbf{k}k at position nnn:

⟨Rmq,Rnk⟩=(Rmq)T(Rnk)=qTRmTRnk \langle \mathbf{R}_m \mathbf{q}, \mathbf{R}_n \mathbf{k} \rangle = (\mathbf{R}_m \mathbf{q})^T (\mathbf{R}_n \mathbf{k}) = \mathbf{q}^T \mathbf{R}_m^T \mathbf{R}_n \mathbf{k} ⟨Rm​q,Rn​k⟩=(Rm​q)T(Rn​k)=qTRmT​Rn​k

Because RmT=R−m\mathbf{R}_m^T = \mathbf{R}_{-m}RmT​=R−m​ and rotations compose additively:

Outcome School

RmTRn=R−mRn=Rn−m \mathbf{R}_m^T \mathbf{R}_n = \mathbf{R}_{-m} \mathbf{R}_n = \mathbf{R}_{n - m} RmT​Rn​=R−m​Rn​=Rn−m​⟨Rmq,Rnk⟩=qTRn−mk \langle \mathbf{R}_m \mathbf{q}, \mathbf{R}_n \mathbf{k} \rangle = \mathbf{q}^T \mathbf{R}_{n - m} \mathbf{k} ⟨Rm​q,Rn​k⟩=qTRn−m​k

The resulting attention score depends solely on (n−m)(n - m)(n−m), yielding relative position encoding directly from an absolute rotation.

Outcome School

2. Generalization to ddd-Dimensional Space

Attention heads have dimension ddd (where ddd is even). RoPE chunks the vector into d/2d/2d/2 consecutive pairs of 2D coordinates:

Baidu AI Cloud

x=[(x1,x2),(x3,x4),…,(xd−1,xd)] \mathbf{x} = \big[ (x_1, x_2), (x_3, x_4), \dots, (x_{d-1}, x_d) \big] x=[(x1​,x2​),(x3​,x4​),…,(xd−1​,xd​)]

Each pair j∈{0,1,…,d2−1}j \in \{0, 1, \dots, \frac{d}{2}-1\}j∈{0,1,…,2d​−1} rotates at a distinct frequency θj\theta_jθj​:

θj=b−2j/d(typically base b=10 000 or higher) \theta_j = b^{-2j / d} \quad (\text{typically base } b = 10\,000 \text{ or higher}) θj​=b−2j/d(typically base b=10000 or higher)
  • Low dimensions (small jjj): High frequencies, fast rotations (captures fine, short-range syntax).
  • High dimensions (large jjj): Low frequencies, slow rotations (captures long-range document context). Machine Learning Mastery

The full rotation matrix RΘ,md\mathbf{R}_{\Theta, m}^dRΘ,md​ is a block-diagonal matrix:

TensorTonic

RΘ,md=diag⁡(Rθ0,m, Rθ1,m, …, Rθd/2−1,m) \mathbf{R}_{\Theta, m}^d = \operatorname{diag}\left( \mathbf{R}_{\theta_0, m}, \, \mathbf{R}_{\theta_1, m}, \, \dots, \, \mathbf{R}_{\theta_{d/2 - 1}, m} \right) RΘ,md​=diag(Rθ0​,m​,Rθ1​,m​,…,Rθd/2−1​,m​)

Efficient Computation (No Dense Matrix Multiply)

Because multiplying by a block-diagonal sparse matrix is wasteful, implementations use element-wise operations with half-vector swaps (rotate_half):

Machine Learning Mastery

RΘ,mx=x⊙cos⁡(mΘ)+x~⊙sin⁡(mΘ) \mathbf{R}_{\Theta, m} \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x} \odot \cos(m\Theta) + \tilde{\mathbf{x}} \odot \sin(m\Theta) RΘ,m​x=x⊙cos(mΘ)+x~⊙sin(mΘ)

where x~\tilde{\mathbf{x}}x~ swaps adjacent pairs and flips the signs:

x~=[−x2,x1,−x4,x3,…,−xd,xd−1] \tilde{\mathbf{x}} = [-x_2, x_1, -x_4, x_3, \dots, -x_d, x_{d-1}] x~=[−x2​,x1​,−x4​,x3​,…,−xd​,xd−1​]

Key Properties

  • Norm Preserving: Because rotation matrices are orthogonal (RTR=I\mathbf{R}^T \mathbf{R} = \mathbf{I}RTR=I), ∥Rx∥=∥x∥\Vert{}\mathbf{R} \mathbf{x}\Vert{} = \Vert{}\mathbf{x}\Vert{}∥Rx∥=∥x∥. The positional transformation does not alter feature magnitude. TensorTonic
  • Long-Distance Decay: As the distance ∣m−n∣\vert{}m - n\vert{}∣m−n∣ grows, the sum over sinusoidal frequencies tends to attenuate the expected dot product value, acting as a natural inductive bias that nearby tokens are more relevant.
  • KV-Cache Friendly: Tokens can be encoded on-the-fly and cached at inference without needing to recalculate past tokens when the context grows.
  • Extensibility: Techniques like YaRN, NTK-aware scaling, and Linear RoPE scaling adjust base frequencies bbb or scale positions mmm to extend pretrained context windows (e.g., from 4k to 128k+ tokens).
